catalog_quote: Ich wende mich daher zum dynamischen wortaccent. Es würde mich zu weit führen, auf eine erschöpfende behandlung desselben einzugehen. Die folgenden angaben beschränken sich auf das allerwichtigste. Die hauptregel ist: die stammsilben tragen den hauptaccent, die nebensilben sind verhältnismässig schwächer. Es lassen sich im allgemeinen etwa vier stärkestufen unterscheiden, die natürlich selbst wider schwankungen unterworfen sind. Ich bezeichne sie mit stark- oder haupttonig (1), mittelstark (2), unterstark (3), schwach oder unaccentuiert (4). Unter 'nebentonig' fasse ich die stufen 2 und 3 zusammen.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Bavarian (bava1246) is not in the catalog. this search of works with stress in the title returned a single title-keyword hit, Schröbler 1957 (PBB 79: 1-42), which the Crossref record confirms is about alliteration in Anglo-Latin 'carmina rhythmica' in the Vienna Boniface manuscript; it is irrelevant to Bavarian word stress (keyword artefact 'rhythmica'), paywalled at De Gruyter, priority none. the De Gruyter page blocks downloads). The best first-hand statement actually read is Schwäbl 1903, Die altbayerische Mundart § 9 p. 13, verified from the page image: the root syllable carries the Hochton (Hauptaccent) and all pre-/post-root syllables are unstressed and reduce (schwa never in stressed stem syllables, p. 14) — i.e. Germanic fixed root-initial stress; Schatz 1897 § 31 p. 28 (Imst, South Bavarian: 'Die Stammsilben tragen den Starkton') corroborates.

new_statements.translation: I therefore turn to the dynamic word accent. It would lead me too far to treat it exhaustively; the following remarks are confined to the most essential. The main rule is: the stem syllables carry the main accent, the secondary (affixal) syllables are comparatively weaker. In general about four grades of strength can be distinguished, which are of course themselves subject to fluctuation. I label them strong or main-stressed (1), medium-strong (2), under-strong (3), weak or unaccented (4).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Main (dynamic) word stress falls on the stem/root syllable (Germanic root-initial stress); prefixes and derivational/inflectional syllables are weaker, graded by vowel quality and rhythm. Concordant statements in Schatz 1897 §31 (Imst), Tschinkel 1908 §36 (Gottschee), Gebhardt 1907 §18 (Nürnberg: native words stem-stressed, unassimilated loans keep source stress, established loans often get Germanic initial stress, first member of compounds strongest) and Schwäbl 1903 §9 (Altbayern).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Lessiak §§44-47: four strength grades; Nebensilben with schwa or syllabic nasal/liquid are weak, those with full vowels (e.g. -haft, -schaft, -bar, -keit, -ung, -lich) 'unterstark'; in trisyllables with unstressed second syllable the third gets a stronger rhythmic Nebenaccent (1:4:3), which preserves full vowels in third-position compound members (Weinbeere) while second-position members reduce; heavy suffix in second position takes the Nebenaccent (1:3:4). Gebhardt §18.4: a Nebenton only in heavy compounds still felt as compounds; otherwise all non-main syllables equally unstressed.
new_statements.exceptions: Gebhardt §18: unassimilated loanwords keep original stress, but established loans are stressed Germanically (khépala 'Kapellchen', Mérkhūr); tautological and comparative adjective compounds have level stress on all members (diksát, grôsgrei). Tschinkel §36: stem stress even where NHG deviates (lantikh 'lebendig', hóldər 'Holunder'); the vowel-weight law is often overridden by rhythm. Schwäbl §9 Anm.: given names often retain Latin stress. Lessiak/Schatz: rhythmic demotion/shift of Nebenton in connected speech.
new_statements.domain_note: Lessiak explicitly treats the 'dynamischer wortaccent' of the word (separately from Silbenaccent §§ before and Satzaccent after); Tschinkel states the rule for 'die Betonung des isolierten Wortes'; all sources note rhythmic adjustments of secondary stress at phrase level, not of the main stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Quoted source (Lessiak 1903) describes the dialect of Pernegg in Carinthia = Carinthian Bavarian [cari1287], a South Bavarian [sout2632] variety of bava1246. Concordant first-hand statements were read and saved for Tyrol South Bavarian (Schatz 1897, Imst; tyro1234), Gottscheerisch (Tschinkel 1908; gott1234), the Nuremberg city dialect which its author assigns to Oberpfälzisch/North Bavarian (Gebhardt 1907; nort2634, transitional to East Franconian), and Altbayern West Central Bavarian (Schwäbl 1903; west2966). No accessible modern description of Central Bavarian states the rule; the modern reference works (Zehetner 1985, Wiesinger 1990, Rowley 1990, Merkle 1975) are print-only.

new_statements.quote: In der deutschen Sprache hat die Wurzelsilbe den Hochton (Hauptaccent); was ihr vorausgeht oder nachfolgt, ist im Tone geschwächt, so daß in Vor-, Nach- und Flexionssilben, ja sogar in sonst selbständigen Wörtern durch ihre Unterordnung unter die Gewalt eines fremden und durch den Verlust des eigenen Hochtones eine Abschleifung der Vokale und überhaupt eine Verstümmelung ihrer vollen Formen entsteht. [...] [p.14:] Daher kommt ə niemals in betonten Stammsilben vor, sondern nur in unbetonten Silben und Wörtern
new_statements.translation: In the German language the root syllable carries the high tone (main accent); whatever precedes or follows it is weakened in tone, so that in prefix, suffix and inflectional syllables, and even in otherwise independent words, through their subordination to the force of a foreign [accent] and the loss of their own main accent, a wearing-down of the vowels and in general a mutilation of their full forms arises. [...] Hence ə never occurs in stressed stem syllables, but only in unstressed syllables and words.
new_statements.citation: Schwäbl, Johann Nepomuk. 1903. Die altbayerische Mundart. Grammatik und Sprachproben. München: Lindauer. § 9, pp. 13-14 (Altbayern, Central Bavarian).
new_statements.locator: § 9, p. 13 (paragraph beginning 'In der deutschen Sprache'), continued p. 14
new_statements.reading: Fixed morphological (root/stem-syllable) stress of the Germanic type: the lexical root syllable, normally word-initial in native words, carries the main accent; prefixes, suffixes, inflections and clitics are unstressed and reduce to schwa. Schwäbl frames the rule as holding for German generally and applies it to the Altbayern dialect (with an Anm. on hypocoristic names truncated to the Latin-stressed syllable: Bertl Albertus, Sepp Josephus, Resi Theresia). Independently corroborated first-hand for South Bavarian (Imst, Tyrol) by Schatz 1897 § 31 p. 28 (scanned text held by the project, line 1861): 'Die Stammsilben tragen den Starkton', with a four-degree gradation (Starkton, starker/schwacher Nebenton, Schwachton) and stressed separable-prefix compounds (úmfallen).
